---
title: "Methodology"
---

## Corpus purpose and scope

A longitudinal corpus examining how Canadian official institutions have represented Haiti and framed Canadian security and intervention in the country from 1991 to 2026. It brings together policy documents, parliamentary records, military and police materials, diplomatic statements, development publications, sanctions, and budget documents to trace changing narratives and practices of security and intervention.

The documentary unit is an official publication or parliamentary sitting, not an individual digitized page. Inclusion does not require any analytical concept. A document enters the corpus when its substantive content develops Canadian policy or action, an operation or mission, assistance, sanctions, diplomacy, testimony, a recommendation, or a meaningful official assessment concerning Haiti. The corpus is therefore focused on security and intervention rather than general Canada–Haiti relations.

## Official sources, discovery, and retrieval

Discovery is restricted to configured official Canadian listings, archives, catalogues, search systems, and APIs. Search results and catalogue notices are discovery aids rather than corpus records: the official document must be retrieved, fall within the temporal scope, and satisfy the substantive-Haiti criterion. HTML and PDF text are extracted locally, while retrieval outcomes and failures remain in diagnostics. Direct document URLs, discovery pages, component URLs, formats, and retrieval metadata are preserved for provenance.

`source` identifies the official connector or collection through which a document was discovered. It may differ from the institution that issued the document. `document_type` identifies the document’s precise administrative or editorial form and is more specific than document family. Source, institution, family, and document type are therefore distinct variables.

Publication dates, page-modification dates, and operation or event dates are stored separately. The analytical year uses an operation’s start date for operation records and otherwise uses the official publication date; uncertain dates remain explicitly uncertain rather than being inferred from unrelated metadata.

## Document identity and official-language versions

Stable `document_id` values identify logical documents. Official English and French versions share a document identity only when authoritative links, publication identifiers, or archival structure establish the relationship; title similarity alone is insufficient. Each version retains its own `version_id`, language, title, URL, and extracted text. A genuinely bilingual publication may remain one bilingual version when the official record cannot be separated reliably.

Historical parliamentary identity uses the parliament, session, publication type, and sitting or report number. Page-level archival components belonging to one publication share a logical identity, while their URLs remain explicit provenance. Consolidated legislation remains distinct from the original regulations and amendments published in the *Canada Gazette*.

## Inclusion, exclusion, and human review

New logical documents enter a durable review table. Human reviewers retain or reject each document and may record notes, reviewer identity, and a timestamp. Decisions apply at the logical-document level and propagate only to its verified official-language versions. The active corpus contains the versions of retained documents; rejected and diagnostically excluded material remains auditable outside it.

Indexes, navigation pages, contents pages, editorial corrections, notices of future discussion, formal adoption of an already retained report, and incidental mentions do not satisfy the substantive-inclusion threshold. Their exclusion does not imply that they lack historical interest outside this corpus.

## Institutions, document families, and types

Institution identifies the public organization officially responsible for issuing or producing a document. It is determined from the official publication page, metadata, or document header, not from organizations merely mentioned in the text.

Institutional classification identifies the official sites where security and intervention concerning Haiti are produced, debated, authorized, financed, implemented, or evaluated. It permits observation of changing responsibility among Parliament, diplomacy, defence, policing, development, and public finance. It classifies observable documentary production, not presumed institutional intent.

Document family is a broad category grouping records by the principal official domain or instrument through which Canadian security and intervention in Haiti are documented. It describes neither the document’s political position nor every subject it contains. A document may belong to more than one family when several domains are substantively represented.

Families are selected for documentary observability, recurrence across documents or periods, longitudinal comparability, and relevance to how security and intervention were debated, authorized, financed, announced, implemented, or evaluated. The active codes in `config/families.csv` are:

- `defence_policy`: white papers, defence policies, strategic statements, and implementation documents;
- `parliament`: parliamentary debates, evidence, reports, motions, and related publications;
- `development`: development and cooperation policies, programs, evaluations, and publications;
- `armed_forces`: Canadian Armed Forces operations, missions, and military archives;
- `rcmp`: RCMP publications and international-policing or police-mission records;
- `statements`: ministerial speeches, statements, news releases, and official readouts;
- `regional_strategy`: official strategies and frameworks concerning the Americas, the Caribbean, or another relevant regional configuration;
- `sanctions`: sanctions regulations, announcements, reviews, and related measures;
- `public_finance`: budgets, estimates, public accounts, and expenditure documents.

Families are not mutually exclusive.

## Analytical concept coding

The controlled bilingual vocabulary identifies explicit security-related concepts in retained official text. Configured regular expressions are matched within Haiti-related paragraphs or sections, stored relevance passages, or bounded contexts around references to Haiti or Haitians. Full stored text may be used only when a document’s title and structure establish that it is devoted to Haiti. A title, institution, family, or document type does not independently generate a concept proposal.

Proposals are consolidated at `document_id + concept`, with English and French evidence preserved separately. Human review confirms or dismisses each proposal. Confirmed concepts are consolidated at the logical-document level, sorted deterministically, and propagated identically to every official-language version.

Four states distinguish the outcome:

- `confirmed`: at least one concept is confirmed;
- `pending_review`: at least one proposal awaits review;
- `reviewed_no_confirmed_concept`: proposals or previous assignments were reviewed, but all were dismissed;
- `no_configured_match`: contextual matching produced no proposal.

The completed corpus contains 150 logical documents: 91 `confirmed`, none `pending_review`, 30 `reviewed_no_confirmed_concept`, and 29 `no_configured_match`. It contains 184 confirmed document–concept relationships. The document table and heatmap use confirmed concepts only; pending documents are not treated as documents with zero concepts.

Documents without a confirmed concept remain because substantive inclusion is determined independently from concept coding. A relevant publication may document operations, expenditures, institutions, or intervention without using the selected vocabulary. Removing such documents would select the corpus according to the concepts being measured, and the absence of a confirmed concept does not prove that the underlying idea is absent.

## Spatial coding

Spatial coding begins with bilingual lexical proposals in Haiti-related context. Occurrences are consolidated at `document_id + dimension + proposed_code`, with English and French evidence preserved separately. Human reviewers confirm or dismiss each proposal. Geographical mentions are rejected when they do not structure the documented action or relationship, including incidental place names, affiliations, administrative boilerplate, or references to an unrelated country.

The completed spatial review contains 156 confirmed and 62 dismissed proposals, with none pending.

The spatial-configuration constellation uses confirmed coding only and counts each logical `document_id` once for a given period and code. It is a schematic, non-geographical view: connection strength represents distinct supporting documents, while position and distance do not represent geographic location or causal importance.

## Engagement coding and dashboard visualizations

The dashboard organizes its analytical views into four lenses: engagements, spatial configurations, discourses and concepts, and institutions and instruments. These lenses reorganize the same reviewed corpus and do not change document inclusion or analytical classifications.

The engagement board is a curated analytical layer over the retained corpus. `engagements.csv` identifies documented Canadian actions, `engagement_documents.csv` links supporting retained documents, and `engagement_instruments.csv` records observable instruments. A `document_id` identifies a publication; an `engagement_id` identifies an action. A publication becomes engagement evidence only when it documents that action explicitly.

The board uses six layers: military operations, police activity, development and institutional support, diplomatic and multilateral action, sanctions and regulation, and financial or humanitarian assistance. One engagement may appear in several layers when several instruments are documented. Points represent engagements rather than documents, and their density is not a measure of intervention intensity.

The layers show the sedimentation, coexistence, and modular combination of documented instruments. Their vertical order implies neither hierarchy nor causal dependence.

Other dashboard views count distinct logical documents and use reviewed document-level institutions, families, dates, languages, and confirmed concepts. Percentages describe the retained corpus rather than external levels of governmental activity.

## Reproducibility, audit trail, and development environment

Configuration files define the case, temporal scope, official sources, document families, and controlled vocabularies. Separate tables preserve candidates, document-review decisions, the retained corpus, concept decisions, spatial decisions, engagement coding, retrieval diagnostics, and validation changes. Stable identities and append-only audit records make reviewed additions, removals, metadata changes, and coding propagation traceable.

The principal public data files are:

- `data/candidates.csv`: content-validated candidate versions;
- `data/review.csv`: authoritative logical-document decisions;
- `data/corpus.csv`: retained official-language versions;
- `data/concept_decisions.csv`: authoritative concept decisions and evidence;
- `data/spatial_review_queue.csv`: consolidated spatial decisions and evidence;
- `data/concepts.csv`: the publishable analytical vocabulary;
- `data/retrieval_diagnostics.csv`: retrieval and validation outcomes;
- `data/validation_changes.csv`: the reconciliation and validation audit trail.

The project is developed in R using the Positron IDE, with OpenAI Codex assisting programming, testing, and documentation. Human researchers remain responsible for corpus review, analytical coding, and methodological choices.
